                               Focal Pedal-Antipedal Area Products
                                        in Elliptic Billiards
                                                    Alper Ferudun∗

                                                    1 October 2026



                                                        Abstract
              We prove constancy of the signed area product of the pedal and antipedal polygons at either
          ﬁxed focus of an elliptic billiard, when the least period is divisible by four and the confocal caustic
          is an ellipse. Convex and primitive star trajectories are included. The argument gives two ex-
          plicit factors: the focal pedal area is a ﬁxed multiple of the outer tangent-polygon area, and the
          focal antipedal area is a ﬁxed multiple of the original area. Their product reduces the assertion
          to Chávez-Caliz’s even-period area-product theorem. A velocity-coordinate telescope and a Jacobi
          quarter-period permutation provide the ﬁrst factor; opposite-edge algebra provides the second. This
          establishes invariant k403,b in the usual genuine-period interpretation, with that convention stated
          explicitly. No absolute priority claim is made.


1        Statement and conventions
Fix a > b > 0, put c2 = a2 − b2 , and consider the boundary and caustic
                               x2 y 2                     x2     y2
                          E:      + 2 = 1,        C:          +       = 1,          0 < λ < b2 .                    (1)
                               a2  b                    a2 − λ b2 − λ
Let P = (P1 , . . . , PN ) be a periodic billiard trajectory on E tangent to C. Throughout, N denotes its
least positive period. We allow every coprime winding number admitted by the elliptic caustic, including
star trajectories. For any ordered polygon set
                                               1∑
                                     A(V ) =       det(Vi , Vi+1 ),     VN +1 = V1 .
                                               2 i

All derived polygons retain trajectory order. Their areas are signed, not sums of absolute areas of
bounded faces.
    Write A = A(P ) and let T be the area of the polygon formed by consecutive intersections of the
tangents to E at Pi . For one ﬁxed focus F = (±c, 0), let p be the area of the pedal polygon whose
vertices are the perpendicular feet from F to the original sidelines. Let q be the area of the antipedal
polygon, whose deﬁning sides are
                                        (Pi − F ) · (X − Pi ) = 0.                                   (2)
The conjecture k403,b in [1, 2, Table 5] asserts constancy of pq for N ≡ 0 (mod 4). Both factors concern
the original orbit at the same focus. The source uses signed areas and expressly permits self-intersecting
antipedals.
    For compact notation put

               α = a2 ,   β = b2 ,   d = α − β = c2 ,    D = αβ,      s = α + β,     J = (α − λ)(β − λ).

                                                            1
Theorem 1. For every primitive billiard family in (1) with N ≡ 0 (mod 4), the same-focus signed
pedal-antipedal product is constant. More precisely,

                                 p = KT,          q = RA,        pq = KR(AT ),                              (3)

where                            √
                                     J(β − λ)               D(3β − α) + λ(α − β)2
                            K=                ,      R=                           .                         (4)
                                       β2                        2D(β − λ)
All consecutive outer and focal-antipedal intersections are ﬁnite. The formulas include zero or negative
antipedal area.

    The source does not expressly expand “N -periodic” into a minimum-period deﬁnition. Its genuine-
family interpretation is used here, and is essential: an arbitrary repeated list of 4m vertices does not
satisfy the quarter-period argument below. Section 6 records an exact control illustrating this distinction.
Neither a hyperbolic caustic nor a degenerate endpoint is included in the theorem.


2    Reﬂection and the focal pedal area
Choose the orientation with the caustic on the left of every directed edge. Its center and both foci lie
strictly inside it, so
                          det(Pi , Pi+1 ) > 0,   det(Pi − F, Pi+1 − F ) > 0.                         (5)
The second inequality already proves ﬁnite consecutive antipedal intersections. Reversal changes every
signed area’s sign and preserves the claimed identities.
    At P = (a cos θ, b sin θ) deﬁne

                                                    (b cos θ, a sin θ)              (−a sin θ, b cos θ)
              W = β cos2 θ + α sin2 θ,        n=          √            ,      t=          √             .
                                                            W                               W
Here n is the outward unit normal, t the positive unit tangent, and det(n, t) = 1. The incoming and
outgoing unit velocities are
                                                                      √                    √
                                                                           W −λ                λ
                    v− = ht + jn,         v+ = ht − jn,         h=              ,     j=         .          (6)
                                                                            W                  W

To see the normal-component formula√      directly, a chord with endpoint parameters u − δ, u + δ has
unit direction (−a sin u, b cos u)/ U , where U = α sin2 u + β cos2 u. Confocal tangency gives sin2 δ =
λU/D, so its squared normal component is D sin2 δ/(U W ) = λ/W . Its positive tangent component and
reﬂection give (6).

The left side telescopes around the orbit: each outgoing velocity is the next incoming velocity. Since
d, λ > 0, the asserted identity follows. No area invariance has been assumed.

3    The outer area and a quarter-period permutation
Set L = D − sλ. For a vertex with boundary parameter θ, the two adjacent half-gap tangents z = tan δ
solve
                              (L + λW )z 2 − 2λd cos θ sin θ z − λW = 0.                        (11)
This follows by substituting u = θ +δ in D sin2 δ = λ(α sin2 u+β cos2 u). The leading coeﬃcient satisﬁes

                                         L + λW ≥ α(β − λ) > 0,

so the roots have opposite signs and are ﬁnite.√One√is the forward half-gap tangent and the other is
minus the backward one. Their diﬀerence is 2 λD W − λ/(L + λW ). The unit-circle tangent-side
area formula, followed by the linear map diag(a, b), therefore gives
                                                      √

4    An opposite-edge formula for the antipedal
Translate the origin to F . Consecutive antipedal sides then have equations u · Z = |u|2 and v · Z = |v|2 ,
where u = P − F , v = Q − F . Collecting adjacent terms in the signed shoelace sum expresses the
                       ∑
antipedal area as q = i E(Pi − F, Pi+1 − F ), with
                                            |u|2 |v|2 − (|u|2 + |v|2 )(u · v)/2
                                E(u, v) =                                       .                       (16)
                                                         det(u, v)
Indeed, if r = |u|, r′ = |v| and η is their oriented normal-angle increment, the grouped term is rr′ csc η −
(r2 + r′2 ) cot η/2. It follows by writing the two intersection coordinates along each oriented side and
collecting half their determinants. The derivation does not require a convex antipedal.
Lemma 4. For any centrally paired elliptic-caustic trajectory, q = RA with R given by (4).
Proof. Write an edge’s endpoint parameters as t − δ, t + δ, and set
                        U = α − d cos2 t,     C0 = cos δ,    S0 = sin δ,     z = c cos t.
Then S02 = λU/D, z 2 = α − U and
                     det(P, Q) = 2abS0 C0 ,       det(P − F, Q − F ) = 2bS0 (aC0 − z).
Use the focal-distance formula |P − F | = a − c cos(t − δ) in (16). Its numerator divided by 2S02 is
                               H(c) = (2β − U )(a − zC0 )2 + U (U − β)S02 .
The opposite edge has c replaced by −c. Combining the two fractions and dividing by det(P, Q) gives

5    The published area theorem and its hypotheses
Chávez-Caliz proves that AT is constant for even-period Poncelet families between concentric ellipses
in general position [3, Theorem 6, p. 104]. Her area deﬁnition is the signed shoelace formula [3, p. 93];
the theorem is not restricted to convex polygons or winding one. Its tangent polygon is precisely the
outer polygon used in (12).
    For (1), general position is automatic. The complex projective conics have four distinct ﬁnite
intersections with
                                       α(α − λ)              β(β − λ)
                                 x2 =           ,    y2 = −           .
                                        α−β                   α−β
Their coordinates are nonzero, and the determinant of their aﬃne gradients equals
                                             4xyλ(α − β)
                                                            ̸= 0.
                                           αβ(α − λ)(β − λ)
There is no common point at inﬁnity, since the two leading diagonal quadratic forms have diﬀerent
coeﬃcient ratios. Hence all four intersections are transverse. No in-domain limiting extension of the
cited theorem is required.
    It follows that AT is constant. Equations (8) and (15) give p = KT , and Lemma 4 gives q = RA.
Since K, R depend only on the ﬁxed ellipse and caustic, Theorem 1 follows.                         □


6    Checks, period scope and provenance
For the standard primitive four-periodic family, λ = D/s, R = 2, K = D/s2 and AT = 8D, so
                                                          16D2
                                                 pq =          .
                                                           s2
For a = 5, b = 3, both the axial diamond and the rectangular member give pq = 202500/289, although
their two factors diﬀer. The supplement includes exact rational/quadratic-ﬁeld geometry checks, in-
cluding crossed antipedals, and coeﬃcientwise polynomial checks of the displayed identities. Rounded
higher-period experiments are corroboration only; no ﬁnite set of phases supplies the general proof.

                                                          5
Remark 5. Least period is a substantive hypothesis. In the same ellipse a = 5, b = 3 with λ = 225/64,
exact primitive six-periodic trajectories starting at boundary half-angle parameters 0 and 1/3 have focal
products
                                          823875          1390594355
                                                    and                ,
                                           1024             1721344
respectively. The supplementary exact checker veriﬁes closure, reﬂection, caustic tangency and both focal
areas. Traversing each twice creates a 12-entry list and multiplies its product by four, without changing
its least period of six. This refutes a padded-list extension, not the genuine-period assertion proved above.
Conversely, repeating an orbit whose least period is divisible by four preserves constancy and scales the
product by the square of the repetition count.

    The ellipse-billiard construction, Jacobi parametrization and even outer-area-product theorem are
prior work and are credited explicitly. The contribution here is the focal pedal bridge and antipedal
factor, with their application to the stated invariant and precise period scope. A bounded primary-
literature search did not identify this exact conclusion, but does not establish originality or absolute
priority.
    This manuscript is an unrefereed preprint. AI assistance was used in derivation, internal checking,
coding and manuscript preparation. There has been no independent human peer review or formal
proof-assistant veriﬁcation. The written argument and cited theorem hypothesis map, not numerical
experiments, establish the result.
